vignette:
Leilani Taufa is a twenty-nine-year-old Tongan-American contemporary dancer who presented for her initial intake following what she described, with visible difficulty, as "everything falling apart at once." She is single, currently living alone in a studio apartment, and had been employed as a company dancer with a mid-sized contemporary ensemble until her attendance became too erratic to sustain. She was referred by her general practitioner after a routine appointment at which she broke down while trying to explain why she had stopped working.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Leilani was attending an outdoor cultural festival in a mid-sized American city - an event she had looked forward to for months, one that celebrated Pacific Islander communities and at which her company was scheduled to perform. She had been standing near the main stage, in a crowd dense enough that she could not easily move in any direction, when a coordinated attack unfolded. The details she has been able to share come in fragments: a sound she initially mistook for a speaker malfunction, then smoke, then the press of bodies surging in every direction while she remained pinned near a barrier, unable to move, unable to see an exit, unable to do anything but wait. She does not have a continuous account of what happened. What she has instead are pieces - a partial image, a physical sensation, an emotional wave that arrives without a picture attached to it - and she has said more than once that not being able to tell the story in order makes her feel as though something is wrong with her mind. The perpetrators were never prosecuted, a fact she returns to with quiet, exhausted bitterness.

In the weeks after the attack, Leilani found herself reorganising her life around what felt, to her, like simple practical logic. Theatres, rehearsal studios, subway cars, elevators - any space where the exits were limited or the walls came close - became places she stopped entering. For a dancer, this was not a peripheral inconvenience. Rehearsals take place in studios. Performances take place on stages inside buildings. Within three months she had declined enough calls from her artistic director that the professional relationship quietly dissolved. She told herself she would return when she felt ready, and she forced herself to hold that thought - to replace what she actually felt with a deliberate, willed optimism - because allowing herself to think otherwise felt unbearable. She has spent considerable time turning the event over in her mind, asking what it was meant to teach her, whether there was a reason it happened to her specifically, as though an answer might make the weight of it more bearable.

What Leilani had not anticipated was how much of her sense of self was bound up in the community that had gathered at that festival. The Tongan and broader Pacific Islander networks she had belonged to - the aunties who came to her shows, the cultural organisations her family had been part of for decades - now felt unreachable. Certain conversation topics common in those circles, and even hearing names associated with people who had been present that day, produce in her an abrupt, disorienting distress she cannot fully explain or predict. She has largely stopped attending community events, and the distance that has grown between her and that world is something she experiences as a kind of bereavement.

At home, Leilani sleeps lightly. She finds herself listening for sounds at the edges of the apartment - footsteps in the hallway, the creak of a door - and when a noise arrives unexpectedly, her body responds before her mind catches up. Strangers who approach her in ordinary settings, a cashier stepping around a counter, a neighbour in the corridor, register to her as threats requiring immediate assessment. She is aware, in the abstract, that this is not proportionate. She has come to believe, in a way she cannot fully articulate, that nothing she does now carries any real weight, that the life she was building has lost its coherence, and that the people responsible for that loss have simply continued on undisturbed.

What finally brought her to seek help was a phone call from her younger sister, who told her plainly that she had become a stranger. Leilani came to her first session hoping, above all, to be able to tell someone what happened - and fearing, most deeply, that she never will.
